title: Perpetual consensus is strong human proof — not divine pastor-authority
source_text: XLI. Itaque quum liber aliquis Scripturae in controversiam vocatur, & dubitatur an vere sit Propheticus & Apostolicus, & cum caetero Canone consignatus ab Apostolis aut viris Apostolicis, agnoscimus optimum hujus rei argumentum duci posse ab Ecclesiae perpetuo & constanti consensu & testimonio, quo liber ille semper relatus est ad Apostolos ut authores sive approbatores, cui testimonio fides derogari non potest, absque magna impudentia atque pervicacia. Nec ullum putamus esse argumentum magis idoneum quo revinci possit homo sectarius, sive haereticus. Nec tamen argumentum istud est divinum, sed humanum, neque vis ejus in eo consistit, quod in Ecclesiae praepositis resideat infallibilis & divina quaedam authoritas. Id enim necesse non est ut argumentum subsistat, & vim suam habeat. Nam in iis qui rem literariam tractant nulla fingi potest talis judicandi infallibilis authoritas. Et tamen perpetuus literatorum consensus qui libros quosdam ascribit Aristoteli, Platoni, & Galeno, sufficit ad plenam fidem faciendam; & si quis contra niti vellet, jure merito protervus & insanus haberetur. Quanto magis ergo consensus Ecclesiae, quam non est dubium peculiari Dei providentia, & Spiritus sancti assistentia regi, fidem faciet librum hunc vel illum ab Apostolo vel Propheta conscriptum, & pro divino commendatum esse.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore when some book of Scripture is called into controversy, and it is doubted whether it is truly Prophetic and Apostolic, and sealed with the rest of the Canon by the Apostles or Apostolic men, we acknowledge that the best argument of this matter can be drawn from the perpetual and constant consensus and testimony of the Church, by which that book has always been referred to the Apostles as authors or approvers — a testimony from which faith cannot be withdrawn without great shamelessness and stubbornness. Nor do we think there is any argument more fit by which a sectarian man, or a heretic, can be refuted. Yet that argument is not divine but human, nor does its force consist in this, that in the overseers of the Church there resides a certain infallible and divine authority. For that is not necessary in order that the argument may stand and have its force. For among those who treat a literary matter no such infallible authority of judging can be feigned. And yet the perpetual consensus of the learned which ascribes certain books to Aristotle, Plato, and Galen suffices to make full faith; and if anyone wished to strive against it, he would rightly and deservedly be held shameless and insane. How much more, then, will the consensus of the Church — which there is no doubt is ruled by God's peculiar providence and the assistance of the Holy Spirit — make faith that this or that book was written by an Apostle or Prophet and recommended as divine.
pass_b_english: So when a book of Scripture is disputed — whether it is truly prophetic and apostolic, and was sealed with the rest of the canon by the apostles or apostolic men — we grant that the best argument is the Church's perpetual, constant consensus and testimony, which has always referred that book to the apostles as authors or approvers.
Faith cannot be withdrawn from that witness without great shamelessness and stubbornness. We know no fitter argument for answering a sectarian or a heretic.
Yet the argument is human, not divine. Its force does not lie in some infallible, divine authority residing in the Church's overseers. That is not required for the argument to stand.

In literary questions no such infallible judging-authority can even be invented; yet the continuous consensus of the learned that ascribes certain books to Aristotle, Plato, or Galen is enough for full confidence, and anyone who fought it would rightly be thought shameless and mad.

How much more, then, does the Church's consensus — which no one doubts is ruled by God's special providence and the Spirit's help — give us confidence that this or that book was written by an apostle or prophet and recommended as divine.
